record.paper_title: Open Questions about Time and Self-reference in Living Systems
record.context_brief: representation as a fundamental biological principle
record.original_question: If representation is treated as a fundamental principle of living systems, how can representation be understood formally rather than merely invoked, and how does representation emerge from molecular-level phenomena where the distinction between a representation and the thing represented appears to disappear?

evidence.quote:
One candidate for such a principle is representation, with representation fundamental to living sys-
tems. But if we take representation as a fundamental principle, we need to understand it as such, rather
than simply invoke it as necessary or convenient. In biology this problem is likely to become one of
reductionism versus emergence as more phenomena come to be understood at the molecular level: at
the level of molecules, representation disappears; how does it emerge? This is another instance of the
coarse-graining problem mentioned previously.

It may be difficult to generalise representation in a formal way, since it covers such a wide range of
phenomena.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Treat "representation" as a candidate fundamental principle of living systems: a relation in which some physical structure or process within an organism stands for, refers to, or carries information about another state of affairs (internal or external). The task is twofold:

(1) Provide a precise formal definition of representation that is general enough to cover the diverse biological phenomena ordinarily called representational (e.g., genetic coding, signal transduction, neural firing patterns, immunological recognition, hormonal signaling), yet restrictive enough to distinguish a representation R of a target T from arbitrary physical correlations or causal couplings between R and T. The definition should specify the carrier, the represented content, the interpreting subsystem (if any), and the conditions under which the representation can misrepresent.

(2) Using this definition, give a mathematical account of how representation emerges from purely molecular-level dynamics in which individual molecules and their interactions exhibit no intrinsic distinction between "representation" and "thing represented." In particular, exhibit a coarse-graining or scale-transition procedure—mapping a microscopic dynamical description (e.g., a stochastic reaction network or molecular-mechanical system) to a macroscopic effective description—under which a well-defined representational relation appears at the macroscopic level but is absent microscopically, and characterize the conditions on the microscopic dynamics necessary and sufficient for such emergence.

Determine whether such a formalization and emergence theorem can be achieved, or prove obstructions showing that no single formal framework simultaneously satisfies (1) and (2) across the full range of biological representational phenomena.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open conceptual/foundational question about how to formalize biological representation and derive it via coarse-graining from molecular dynamics. No general accepted formal theory exists; related programs (biosemiotics, predictive processing, information-theoretic approaches to teleosemantics, free-energy principle) offer partial frameworks but none provides a verified emergence theorem from molecular dynamics. Status appears open.

status_evidence.title: Open Questions about Time and Self-reference in Living Systems
status_evidence.snippet: Lists representation as a candidate fundamental principle requiring formalization and an account of emergence from the molecular level.
status_evidence.claim: The question is explicitly framed as open, requiring a formal account of representation and its emergence.
